body.text: Victoria's royal commission into corruption in the construction sector is underway
The royal commission into corruption in Victoria's construction sector has begun with its first open hearing in Melbourne.
The hearing, in the Melbourne Magistrates' Court, has addressed the inquiry's terms of reference, and is expected to detail the next steps before witnesses are called at later hearings.
Former South Australian Supreme Court chief justice Christopher Kourakis is heading up the commission, which has a budget of $50 million.
Today he said the royal commission's most important duty was to recommend "legal, structural, industrial and cultural reforms" for the construction industry.

He vowed the commission would not be "just one more in an endless series of investigations into the integrity of the industry — that requires much more than removing today's bad actors from the stage and ensuring that they never return".

"I assure the people of Victoria, and warn all people who have done wrong, that the commission will leave no stone unturned in search for whatever is hidden — or whomever lurks underneath it," Mr Kourakis said.
"Anyone who has an ambition to remain in the industry will be better served by early, voluntary disclosures to the commission than by waiting to be found out."
Associate to the commissioner Peter Tantalos earlier kicked off proceedings by reading out a long letters patent that established the inquiry and its scope.

Since at least 1980 there had been "persistent allegations of consistent and criminal conduct in connection with major public and civil infrastructure construction projects across Australia", he said.

Mr Tantalos the terms of reference included investigating "blackmail, bribery and dishonest, bullying, intimidatory, menacing, harassing, discriminatory, misogynistic, threatened or violent behaviour" on major public infrastructure projects in Victoria including those of the government's signature Big Build initiative.
The royal commission will also investigate circumstances where there had been a lack of adherence to proper process, improper influence, favouritism or nepotism, he said.

Assisting counsel Chris Young KC told the commission that allegations "about what was done and was not done" reached from sheds at worksites to union offices, boardrooms, government departments and ministerial offices.
"Corruption is often described as a crime without victims. That is not what we have been told,"
Mr Young gave several examples of incidents alleged to have occurred, including a small Indigenous-owned labour hire business who he said wrote to the minister and the premier in April 2022.
"They said they'd been threatened with violence and banned from sites on a state project. They said they had recordings. They asked for help," he said.
"It is reported that they got a reply a year later, which referred them elsewhere."

In another incident, a woman working in traffic management on a new public hospital said she was locked in a storeman by a man recently released from prison for stalking and threatening children, Mr Young said.
"She says he smoked ice and blew the smoke in her face," he said.
"She reported it. She says that what happened next was she lost her job."
Other workers reported they no longer had jobs on a state tunnel project because they belonged to the wrong union, Mr Young said.
'Violent, hateful and greedy rabble'
Ben Carroll called the royal commission in his first act as premier in July, promising an exhaustive inquiry into the corruption allegations "as soon as possible".
"The terms of reference are broad. They are expansive. Nothing is off limits," he said last month.
They include the extent of corruption on major infrastructure projects, the effectiveness of oversight from government bodies and actions contractors took to mitigate risks.
Mr Carroll committed to the royal commission after toppling his predecessor Jacinta Allan, who had long refused to call an inquiry despite internal pressure.
The Victorian opposition has persistently criticised the terms of reference, saying they allowed former premiers Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan to avoid being hauled before the commission.
However, Mr Carroll rejected the suggestion Ms Allan or Mr Andrews would not be called, having confirmed that ministers and former premiers would be fair game under the terms.
"Anyone and everyone can be called. These are the most comprehensive, broadest terms possible," he said in August.
"We're going to make sure that we leave no stone unturned."
The royal commission comes after an explosive report into the CFMEU released by the Queensland Commission of Inquiry in February.
In it, author Geoffrey Watson SC alleged the Victorian branch of the CFMEU descended into a "violent, hateful and greedy rabble" under former boss John Setka.
Mr Watson estimated that the actions of the CFMEU had cost the Victorian taxpayer around $15 billion — a figure that was strongly disputed by Ms Allan at the time.
Mr Watson said the terms of reference for the royal commission were "really excellently done" and he dismissed criticism by the Victorian opposition.
"I think they're very well designed, quite targeted, and sufficiently specific," he said.
"I think it's a mistake for people to go out and start undermining confidence in the commission before it starts.

"After all, this is a process through which we're hoping the confidence in government will be rebuilt. Now, why criticise it at this time? I do not know why, and I might make another point: the criticism is incorrect."
The commission is expected to report to the state government by August next year.
